item.title: Translating Between Fever Dreams and Internet Memes: An Interview with Li Xianglong
item.dc:creator: Joshua Moore
item.description:
Had Albert Camus managed to live long enough to doomscroll through Instagram and XiaoHongShu, he would have become deeply intrigued by the work of Li Xianglong.

 



 

Born in China and based in Brooklyn, Li’s paintings incorporate familiar characters from popular reaction images or beloved movies, only to place them in playfully unsettling moments. Reminiscent of half-remembered fever dreams and eerily relatable memes, Li’s artwork is undeniably absurd yet incredibly approachable, carrying traces of both Chinese and Western pop culture.

 

 

Although contradiction, distortion, and mistranslation cast an inescapable shadow over these images, Li's unique style of observation and humor skillfully draws his viewers deeper into this strange world.

   

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Colleen Dalusong: A few years ago, you had a video series called Learning Chinese in which you use memes to explain Chinese idioms to English speakers. When I watched Learning Chinese, I could see how it echoes the compositions and subject matter in your paintings. Can you talk about how this series came about? 

Li Xianglong: I was painting a lot when I started the MFA program at the School of Visual Arts [SVA], but our cohort was really unlucky because that was the year of the COVID-19 pandemic. We weren’t allowed into the studios or any of the SVA buildings, so I thought, “Okay, what else can I do in my small apartment?” I had my laptop there, so I learned how to use 3D software like Sketchup to make weird animated versions of what I normally would paint on canvas. It was an unfamiliar tool, but I thought it was a good experience for me as an artist because I learned a lot about my own visual language. The concepts and logic in my videos are very similar to what’s in my paintings. 

CD: On the topic of visual language, you tend to use internet memes in your paintings from both Chinese and Western social media. When I’ve shown your work to my white American colleagues, a lot of them mentioned how approachable it is. You’re using imagery that’s very recognizable, but it’s not kitschy or stereotypical, and most importantly you’re not necessarily commanding the audience to feel a certain way. At the same time, your paintings do function like memes because it’s familiar yet completely open to interpretation, so it helps people reach a realization about their own state of mind. 

LX: That’s what I want, for people to experience this message when they see my painting. I feel like I’m always putting on an act when I go out into the real world. There’s Xianglong the painter, Xianglong the gallerist, Xianglong the boyfriend, and Xianglong the coworker; but who is Xianglong? Does a person’s real self only come out when they’re alone, where there’s nobody to hear or see them? I’m always asking myself this question whenever I’m alone because I want to figure out who I am. I don’t have an answer to this, so I try to figure it out through painting. I want to make my paintings more readable but dreamlike so that more people can resonate with the image and start to think more about the question of “who am I?” 

CD: So you feel like there’s a core self that is untouched by all of these labels, and you’re trying to get to the center of your identity? 

LX: Yes, I’m trying to find another side to myself. 

CD: Out of everyone I’ve met so far, you have one of the more pragmatic outlooks on being an artist. I remember the first time we met, you said that artists should try to make a living beyond selling their art, and that having a non-art industry job always helps. It’s not a romantic thing to say, so it’s not really what most people would want to hear, but it feels true if you want to stay in New York and financially support yourself. 

LX: I honestly don’t really care if my paintings are a huge success sales-wise. As long as I enjoy myself while I’m creating something, that’s what’s most important. And I try to tell my other artist friends to try getting a real job and make friends who aren’t in art because when you’re only around other artists your worldview becomes so narrow. Your art suffers because you’re too immersed in one kind of environment and don’t know anything else about what’s going on in the world. 

CD: I know what you mean. There’s definitely some people who need to get their heads out of the e-flux articles and actually learn how to hold a real conversation. That being said, you do sell a lot of your paintings. When I wanted to include Guardian Spirit in an exhibit last October, you told me it had already sold to a collector in China so I had to pick a different painting. 

LX: Oh yeah, my dealer told me that my main audience seems to be from Guangdong. I think it’s because my paintings are very readable to them since I get so much inspiration from Hong Kong movies. I’m always revisiting my favorite movies, and each time it’s like I’m watching something new. Maybe it’s because I’m now at a different age, or because I gained new knowledge or experience since the last time I watched those movies. 

CD: Your paintings remind me of tattoos in the sense they function as emotional bookmarks. I know a lot of people who have tattoos that they got when they were younger, and they say they wouldn’t pick that specific design now, but they’re still glad they have the tattoo anyways because it’s a visual reminder of how they felt at that point in their life. Your paintings seem to serve a similar purpose for you and your own experiences. But while we’re on the topic, what’s your favorite movie? 

LX: Ah, I don’t know the English name… it’s called 无间道. 

CD: Oh, Infernal Affairs! Wow. That’s so you, I’m not surprised. 

LX: You think so? 

CD: So many of your paintings have machetes and fire and gangster characters in them. I can’t believe I didn’t piece it together until now. Okay so in that case, can you break down the story behind Swim Around? 

LX: The story behind this is pretty crazy. The reference photo is from when I was in high school in China, and my friends and I were playing with a machete in front of the school. In the back you can see the school ranking. 

CD: Oh, they do the same thing in the Philippines. They show pictures of who the top students are, right? 

LX: Yeah! So then there are these good students who are going to have a prosperous future, and they’re just in the background watching us. Then there are the bad students playing around without really caring about what happens next. I took the photo because it just felt so absurd to me. It must have been over 10 years ago now. 

CD: You told me before that your favorite writer is Albert Camus. I can definitely see how absurdism influences your paintings, even in more recent ones like The Moment. Can you talk more about that specific work?

LX: There’s Vegeta from Dragon Ball as a businessman, and he’s really happy in the moment. But he doesn’t realize that behind him is a UFO on fire that could crash into him when he’s not expecting it. You can see the two aliens in the UFO, and the reference picture is from when my girlfriend and I were dancing at a rave during New Year’s Eve. So the businessmen and the aliens are both happy and enjoying the moment, even though there’s a chance that all three of them could die at any time. I just wanted to capture this absurd but joyful moment. Life is strange, but you should just enjoy yourself whenever you can. 

CD: You seem to include a lot of your friends and loved ones in your paintings. Do they ever give you feedback? 

LX: I have this one friend who has a 9-5 job working for a big company. One night after we drank together he said that he can really feel the message I’m trying to express through my paintings. 

CD: And how did he interpret the message in your paintings?

LX: He said it made him think about how everyone has two sides — there’s the side that wants to act like a good, law-abiding citizen in society, but there’s the other side that wants to break the rules and get into dangerous situations. That’s what he told me, at least.

item.title: Behind the Scenes of Grimes’ MV “Miku-Maxxing”: Presented by sabukaru and GATA
item.dc:creator: Joshua Moore
item.description: Grimes and Hatsune Miku’s new song “Miku-Maxxing” BTS with sabukaru and GATA
item.content:encoded:
Airy synths that take the shape of clouds and vocals that soar along electropop melodies, Grimes crafted that ethereal sound you hear in music everywhere nowadays with her own hands. A nod to the internet culture she inspired, she teamed up with Hatsune Miku and Japanese Vocaloid producer SatapanP for her latest single “Miku-Maxxing.”

Grimes’ Visions (2012) and Art Angels (2015) impact cannot be stated enough. Whether it’s her do-it-yourself attitude by producing her own tracks or the electronic textures that she pushed from their homes of ambient and industrial music into a poppier space, Grimes did what felt right to her.

Instead of just taking her own spin on what was hot at the time, Grimes' recontextualization and swirl of inspirations that are authentic to her made her music so fresh. It’s influences like the band Skinny Puppy, an electro-industrial band from her hometown of Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, that are a marquee example of her unique perspective.

  View fullsize
View fullsize
View fullsize
View fullsize
 

Fellow internet girl, the beloved blue-haired icon, Hatsune Miku, set the standard for vocaloid culture today. Created by Crypton Future Media in 2007, Hatsune Miku is a voicebank that can be used to make music. Her popularity arose in the online of niconicovideo [ニコニコ動画] where independent users would upload videos using her software to make music. Since then, she’s spread all across mainstream media in Japan as well as abroad with vocaloid music legends like wowaka citing Miku as their inspiration to start making music.

Presented by sabukaru and GATA, we got an inside look at the filming of the music video, produced by our creative agency Bianco Bianco, that pairs two legends of internet culture. Radiating kindness and courteousness, Grimes worked through a long shoot with ease. That led to such a beautiful, finished video: glitching through the Miku-matrix; regal halls with Hatsune Miku’s signature blue; and poses that jump through the screen.

   

Talking with sabukaru and GATA on set, Grimes spoke about her appreciation for Japan and the dedication of Japanese teams. We also captured the production in motion, meeting the crew such as the music video Director Valley and the Director of Photography Yutaka.

Check out the music video, now live on YouTube.

item.title: FW26 and the Archaeology of Formative Desire: sabukaru Meets Hyein Seo
item.dc:creator: Abeer S
item.description: sabukaru premieres HYEIN SEO’s FW26 collection with an exclusive interview.
item.content:encoded:
Hyein Seo is one of the most consequential figures in Korean fashion, a Royal Academy of Fine Arts Antwerp alumna whose return to Seoul coincided with a period of profound change in the city’s creative culture. More than a decade into HYEIN SEO, the label has evolved with Hyein’s own changing perspective, allowing each collection to reflect the ideas, references and ways of dressing that feel most relevant to her. FW26, premiering on sabukaru, marks the latest chapter in that evolution.

 

 

sabukaru spoke with Hyein about the decade behind that shift, beginning with Antwerp, where the Royal Academy taught her to consider the world surrounding a garment and exposed her to radically different ways of approaching the same idea. Her early collections often began with fictional characters because imagining an actual wearer still felt distant. Seoul changed that, giving those clothes bodies, personalities and lives beyond the studio.

FW26 turns toward the cultural memory carried by Hyein and the five designers in her atelier. Looking back at the figures they admired before fashion became a profession, the team began tracing how those early encounters with music, manga and style had remained embedded in their tastes decades later. Faye Wong, Avril Lavigne and other figures from late-90s and 2000s pop culture became points of departure for the collection, united by the individuality that made them magnetic. The collection brings those memories into 2026, allowing formative images from adolescence to return in altered form.

 

 

Photographed in Japan by Taito Itateyama across three days, the lookbook unfolds inside the spaces where Taito and his friends already spend their time. Hyein missed the expressions that disappear once too many people are watching: laughter that arrives unprompted, gestures made between friends and the ease that only appears when the camera briefly recedes. Watching those relationships unfold, she felt the clothes finally come alive.

 

You studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts Antwerp, which has a very defined legacy and visual code. What stayed with you from your time there, and how did you build your own perspective alongside it?

It’s a notoriously demanding school, but I think it teaches you to see the whole picture, not just how to make clothes. More than anything, it helped me find my own way of expressing ideas.

I also learned a lot from watching the other students. Everyone came from very different backgrounds, and I was always interested in why someone might approach the same assignment in a completely different way.

I think creative work comes from everything a person has absorbed over time, culture, images, stories, all filtered through their own way of seeing and thinking. Even if we are all looking at the same things, that filter is different for everyone, and I think that’s what gives the work its own character.

I was always obsessed with stories, novels and films, so I often built collections around a character or narrative. I wasn’t very good at speaking during presentations, so once I drew the entire story on a long scroll of paper and unrolled it in front of the teachers. That was when they finally understood what I was trying to say. Looking back, that was probably part of finding my own language too.






You spent years between Antwerp and Seoul before fully relocating. You were also part of an earlier wave of designers shaping Seoul’s creative direction. Looking back across your collections, what do you think has changed most about the way you approach design today?

I started the brand with work I had made as a student, so in the beginning I was naturally drawn to clothes with a strong visual impact. They had enough energy to catch your eye even on a small screen like Instagram, and maybe because of that, they reached a lot of musicians and artists.

But some of those clothes had already done their job after being worn once or twice. I know fashion can look dated after a year, and that is part of what I do. Still, it sometimes made me sad to think that a piece might be worn only once or twice and then never picked up again.

With time and experience, I became more interested in everyday clothes. I still want them to have character and a clear statement, but I also want them to stay with the person wearing them for a long time. I started thinking more about the time a garment spends with someone.

Seoul probably had some influence on that too. After moving back, I found a close group of creative friends who constantly influence one another. In the beginning, it was hard to imagine who would actually wear my clothes, so I often started with fictional characters from novels or films. Now I think much more about real people wearing the clothes while they work, run, dance, sing or simply live in them.






How has having a permanent space changed the way you think about presenting your work and engaging with people directly?

We have a small building with the store on the first floor and the atelier above it. There were financial reasons for choosing that setup, but at first I didn’t really like having the two spaces so close together. I thought it might be distracting.

The way a designer’s working process is presented in the media can look quite beautiful, but the reality isn’t always like that. During deadlines, we barely sleep or eat properly and usually look exhausted. At first, I wondered what was good about showing that side of things.

Now I’m used to it, and I think the advantages are much greater. I can see how customers react when I pass through the store, and we can communicate very closely with the store team. We also hear sales feedback quickly and can reflect it in the work.

Having a space, even a small one, where we can show the entire collection has also become a new kind of pleasure for me. Now, when I start a collection, I also think about the space, the music, and the overall atmosphere. It has led me to collaborate more with people from other fields.

I’m only talking about the good parts, but it has definitely created more work too.

HYEIN SEO moved from what was often described as “street couture” into something more wearable and craft-focused. Was that shift driven by your own perspective changing, or by a reaction to the broader fashion system?

I don’t think there was a moment when I consciously decided to change direction. If I had kept repeating the same style from ten years ago, I’m not sure the brand would still exist today. Graphics or slogans can feel fresh at first, but when they are repeated in similar ways, people eventually get tired of them.

I have always liked handmade details and craft. In the past, I think I expressed them in a more direct and visually strong way. Now I’m more interested in how they can appear through materials, construction, and smaller details.

Times change, people change, and I change too. I don’t think the shift came from reacting to the fashion system. It feels more like the result of following what interests me at that moment and trying not to repeat the same thing. Whenever someone defines HYEIN SEO as one particular style, I usually feel like moving a little further away from it.


FW26 draws from the musicians, characters, and pop culture figures you admired growing up. Looking back now, what do you think those early influences gave you creatively that you still carry into your work today?

At the beginning of the collection, I was chatting with the five designers I work with and asked each of them who the first woman or style icon they really admired was. There is a bit of an age gap between us, so the answers came from different generations. What surprised me was how clearly those choices were still reflected in the way they dress, design and even in the attitudes they value.

There was Chara, Faye Wong, Avril Lavigne and Devon Aoki. One person chose a character from a Japanese manga from that period. They were all strong, self-assured characters. At least in our atelier, I don’t think anyone grew up admiring the good girl or the elegant, quiet type.

Japanese fashion and culture from the 2000s also had a major influence on our team. I spent my teenage years looking at magazines like FRUiTS and TUNE. At the time, it felt like every girl was reading Ai Yazawa’s manga. A lot of people probably became designers because of her work. I still remember seeing Namie Amuro on MTV for the first time. She felt completely new to me, and I thought she was incredibly cool.

The people you admire when you are young stay with you more deeply than you realize. They affect how you dress, what you find cool, and the kind of attitude you are drawn to. This collection became a way of looking back at how those influences stayed in our memories, and how they have changed and taken on a new form in 2026.

It was also my first time shooting with a K-pop musician, and I asked Chaeyoung for a similar reason. I had always felt that she had a real interest in underground culture, with a punk and rebellious side to her. She said yes right away, which I really appreciated.

The FW26 lookbook was photographed in everyday spaces with friends instead of a conventional production setting. Why was that approach important to the collection, and what did it allow you to capture that a traditional fashion shoot couldn’t?

As the brand grew, and the photographers I worked with grew too, the scale of our shoots became bigger. I liked that we could create bold images that would have been impossible with a smaller production. But when there are many people watching, the models naturally become a little more self-conscious. Even when they are friends, it can be difficult to show a real expression.

Fashion shoots also come with limits of time and budget. At some point, I started missing the kind of photographs that come from real moments. I wanted the laughter, gestures and emotions that appear while people are talking or playing, instead of expressions made specifically for the camera.

I have known Taito for a few years. I had always liked the rough and wild quality of his photographs, and I really wanted to work with him for this collection.

I went to Japan with musician friends from Korea, and Hidaka and Mayuri joined us there. Taito already had a close relationship with the people in the photographs. Because of that, they were comfortable showing sides of themselves that only come out around people they trust.

We spent two nights and three days shooting around Taito’s neighborhood, almost as if we were simply hanging out. Watching their conversations, the way they looked at each other, and the way they laughed in the wind, I felt the clothes finally came alive on them.



What do you hope people feel when they wear HYEIN SEO, and what kind of confidence or perspective do you hope the clothes give them?

There is an image I always keep in mind when I make clothes and images: someone grounded, looking far ahead. I think I have always been drawn to women who face what is coming with a sense of strength.

I think a lot about posture when I design. I like the idea that wearing the clothes might make someone feel a little more composed and a little stronger, maybe even as though they can get through whatever comes their way.

About the Author: 
Abeer Salah is a Seoul-based editor, writer, and cultural curator exploring emerging scenes, underground culture, and internet-born subcultures. She is the founder of the collective P.T.S.D.

item.title: Gen Z Thinks You’re An Unc: Gen Z’s Obsession with Age
item.dc:creator: Joshua Moore
item.description:
Once you reach the prehistoric age of 22 years old, give up on your dreams. That’s been the mantra of online discourse for Zoomers, a nickname for people who were born between 1997 and 2012, aka Gen Z. This development is rather new. No longer are we in the times that Vincent Van Gogh could pick up a paintbrush for the first time at 27 or Kim Gordon could start playing the bass and guitar at 27. Now, you have to blow up at 16, or you’re forever doomed according to those online.

 


 

Where has this ticking time bomb come from for Gen Z? Perhaps from the fear of failure as social media amplifies social judgement and self-conscious feelings? Or is it the looming financial nightmare of an unsuccessful artistic career with the unforgiving prices of basic needs like rent, food, and transportation?

Looking at online communities like underground rap forums such as the sadboys and ReptilianClubBoyz reddit pages, we chose these communities because these ideals are common in them. They also use the vocab associated with these ideals to connect with each other such as unc with a negative connotation, separate from the origination of the word in the African-American community that holds a neutral connotation.  These forums showcase both the impact of social judgement and financial barriers through the nihilism baked into their humor.

   

From the reddit user Delectablemelons on the ReptilianClubBoyz reddit page, they said “a group of teenagers walked past me and laughed. Was taking my dog out for a walk then ts happened i feel so unc and chopped im only 21 it was so embarrassing is this what it’s like to be a loser hell i even set my alarm at 4 in the morning in the hopes of making less interactions.” The nihilistic mentality of being doomed at 21, avoiding others in fear of judgement or being less than rings both of comedy and despair. The flurry of self-deprecative humor reflects the sentiment in Gen Z that achieving their dreams or acting as one’s authentic self is seen as a far-fetched reality. The despair in these words relays the isolative and depressive impact of social judgement and the lack of socioeconomic mobility in today’s youth.

   

The pervasiveness of social media infects the mind with a constant seeking of approval and hyperawareness of others’ judgement which leads to a multitude of negative reactions such as people retreating into their shell or changing how they represent themselves to fit into an easily consumable package for others. That downsizing and reduction of oneself makes it so that they don’t even know the self. When you don’t know the self and don’t receive outside positive reinforcement, it’s easy to fall into a downward spiral into the dark pits of depression that appear both undefeatable and all-consuming. This spiral leads to a creative psychosis that has people believing that they must throw in the towel, that they must give up their dreams, that there is no point in trying to achieve what they see when they close their eyes.

   

Using a metaphor of a race, the spiral assumes others are too far ahead to catch up to. The psyop of life is that it is a race. It is not a race. It is a journey of the self, completely irrelevant to anyone else’s timeline. This idea that growth ends at a certain age is dangerous. The person that stops growing dies in that very instant, even if they are still breathing.

Perpetual change, regardless of direction or speed, is the essence of life. To stay static is what the confines of capitalism want. Those in power want you to convert into a consumerist role. This is the final stage of consumerism where you solely live to take another breath because, if you break out of this psychosis, the system can no longer control your decisions. Once you realize you and only you are in control of your decisions, that you are all-powerful and that any life can be yours if you start taking steps towards it, you are unstoppable. A specific journey is not promised. A specific life is not promised. A specific result is not promised. What is promised is that different decisions lead to change. So dust off your shoes; the journey is far from over.

item.title: The Sound of Being Online: Sabukaru Meets Ninajirachi
item.dc:creator: Yuuki Hayashi
item.description:
sabukaru caught up with Ninajirachi mid-tour across North America; our conversation moved across gaming, otaku culture, the architecture of a perfect drop, and what it means to build something genuinely personal inside a music world that rewards surface-level spectacle. Nina has built one of the more distinct positions in Australian electronic music, starting from FL Studio sessions in her Central Coast bedroom and arriving at Coachella and sold-out nights across Japan through a sound that has stayed consistent. Her music sits somewhere between maximalist EDM energy and something far more internet-native, grounded by songwriting that carries genuine emotional weight alongside the production. Her studio album I Love My Computer brings that together most directly, a record that is precise in its production and personal in its writing, moving between high energy and genuine emotional openness in a way that has connected with listeners well beyond the electronic music world.

   

INTERVIEW

MIKE SUNDAY: Great, how's it going?
Nina: Going good. How are you?

MIKE SUNDAY: Yeah, really good. It's nice to meet you. We actually met once upon a time in Toronto at one of your shows. I stuck around. I don't know if it was at The Drake or the Velvet Underground. It was like a super small venue.
Nina: At the Drake? In 2024, was it?

MIKE SUNDAY: 2024, believe it or not. I think you had said it was your first tour in North America, but I'm not sure.
Nina: Yeah at the Velvet Underground! my god nice to see you!

MIKE SUNDAY: Yeah, nice to see you. A lot has changed for you since then. So I'm excited to get into it. Where are you calling in from, by the way? Are you in North America right now?
Nina: I'm in the green room in the venue in Dallas. We're playing a show here tonight.

MIKE SUNDAY: I know that for a lot of the things you're into, and the things I'm into, and the people who might be reading this, Japan is kind of the Mecca. I know it wasn't your first time, but you just went on tour in Japan. How was the reception? How are the crowds in Japan? Are there any sort of palpable differences between the crowds in Japan or North America per se?
Nina: Yeah, it was an amazing tour. It was so awesome. It was really fun to do it with the Heaven's Gate crew and Ramon Pang as well. They curated such a cool lineup every night in every city. I also got to play at the Ghost in the Shell exhibition in Tokyo as well. Oh my god, it was so awesome. Like such an honour. Especially getting to go in early and check out the exhibition too. It was sick. The Japan crowd went hard. So there were two Tokyo shows and I noticed that there were a lot of the same people at both shows. The second show, they went a little harder, maybe because they felt like they were able to, or they were very polite and maybe the second night they felt like they had more permission to open the pit and stuff. It was awesome.

   

MIKE SUNDAY: That's great. Did you have a favorite bite there while you were there? I saw some of the photos that were being shared, especially by Ramon and it looks so fun. Were there any memorable meals?
Nina: My god, too many. Honestly, going out with the Heaven's Gate crew, all of those meals were the most special because it was very communal. We were also eating their favourite foods at their favourite spots that I wouldn't have known about as a tourist.

MIKE SUNDAY: I know it's one of those tricky things where even though English is pretty widely spoken, you still kind of need to be able to speak Japanese to kind of get into some of the lesser known spots. So you had talked about Ghost in the Shell. When I look at your lyrics and I hear your music, I definitely get Ghost in the Shell, I get Lain and even FLCL to a certain degree, but is there like an anime specifically that you could just go on about for like hours and hours on end? Do you have that special show?
Nina: I mean, maybe the ones that you mentioned, especially because they deal with some similar themes that I like to write about in my music. Simulations and representations of human experiences and stuff. But when I was little, the first anime I ever watched was either Sailor Moon or Yu-Gi-Oh! There was a lot of anime on TV before school. That was how I discovered it. Because there was an Australian TV channel that would also play the Bakugan anime and a bunch of others before school. So that was my breakfast time watching before I went to school when I was like five or six.

MIKE SUNDAY: That's a pretty formative experience. I actually hit up Ramon to see if there were any sort of insider questions I could maybe get you with. In interviews you often talk about your pop music references. You're [a popstar] level in my opinion and I think a lot of people would say so too. Whether you agree with that or not. But one thing we had chatted about is your love for all sorts of IDM. Maybe some of these artists that don't get enough shine like Igloo Ghost, X&G, Oli XL. Are there any artists you wanna just take the time to gush about and really give them some shine?
Nina: My god, well all of those artists you just mentioned are amazing and so famous to me, like my favourite artists. There's a lot of amazing Australian electronic music. For example, Laces and KAVARI, I just toured with them in the UK. Laces is Australian and we've been friends for like 10 years and his music is just amazing and so detailed. Kenta204 as well, who I've actually released a bunch of [music with] we've got a few songs out together. He's also Japanese Australian as well. There's a lot of really sick producers in Australia and in that scene in general. I remember Ramon and I talking about it. We had a lot of SoundCloud chats when we were on tour together as well. We didn't get enough time together. Really we had the shows and we had dinners, but we could talk about that all day long.

   

MIKE SUNDAY: Do you feel like there's really been a replacement for that sort of SoundCloud culture? It really does feel like what was happening at that time was really special. Have you found something, whether it's through Discord or anything, or was SoundCloud just a place and a time and you had to really be locked in there?
Nina: No, SoundCloud is alive and well. My god. I find so much music through my friends' SoundCloud likes or people's mixes that they upload to SoundCloud and even like Jane [Remover] with the Leroy music. That's a whole world in and of itself that exists on SoundCloud. A lot of artists have alt accounts as well that they upload to on there. I feel like the edit culture is definitely alive and well. Maybe it's a little more on Bandcamp now than it used to be. But I still spend a lot of time on SoundCloud and find heaps of music on there.

MIKE SUNDAY: I think that's a great segue into your insane Coachella run. Congrats on that! Even between Pinkpanthress, underscores all the sort of crazy cameos, perhaps most impactful for you was Porter Robinson? I actually read somewhere that you were involved in one of his fan communities early on, or did I make that up completely?
Nina: I've been a fan for a really long time since. The first song I heard by him was maybe, Language or Easy. And that was when I was like 12 or 13. I went to his show when I was 13 or 14 and that was my first live music experience.

MIKE SUNDAY: Whoa, that's crazy. It’s pretty wild to be a collaborator now or working with them. How does that feel?
Nina: Crazy, yeah. Yeah, it's awesome. I'm so stoked that he likes my music. I'm so happy that like, you know, he's, I'm trying to think of how to word this, especially without sounding weird. He has inspired me for a really long time and he's one of the reasons I got into electronic music. For him to like what I've done with the inspiration he's given me is all I could want to really. Yeah, I'm super flattered by it.

   

MIKE SUNDAY: Yeah, that's evident, that's awesome! Comparing Japan versus Coachella and the bigger festivals, are there different levels of trust? I know some people prefer the smaller rooms because you can get a little bit more experimental, but how do you approach those different sets? What's the mode of mixing there?
Nina: It's a good question. Do you mean like to like a bigger crowd versus like one where people are closer to you and stuff like that? I guess, you know, in a festival setting, perhaps not everyone's there for you. They might be there for a number of reasons, or they only want to hear the hits. Whereas someone who might have gone out and saw you at a smaller venue is looking to hear more deep cuts, or maybe they're there for your taste as opposed to just hearing the hits. I'm curious, do you feel like the pressure to only play hits when you're at Coachella or is that something you can kind of thread the needle with?
Nina: I tried to thread the needle but another consideration is the time because festival sets are a little shorter so when I'm touring around at the moment doing headline shows I'm usually playing like kind of an hour 20-ish long sets. Then at a festival like Coachella for example it is 50 minutes so I was trying to really cram. I was cramming for sure so like at my shows there's some songs that I would usually let breathe a lot more or have longer peaks and valleys perhaps. At Coachella I was really trying to speed run my discography so I made a lot of edits to fit as many songs as I could.

MIKE SUNDAY: Yeah, just freak the energy. Speaking of speed, a lot of music’s success nowadays is really propagated by TikTok and these sort of like TikTok edits. You and I obviously know it as nightcore and this sort of culture of pitching up the vocals and stuff like that. Why do you think it's so appealing? Like, what is it about it that people just like? Especially mixed with sort of the anime aesthetic?
Nina: It's a good question. I'm not sure. I feel like I was born into Nightcore existing. When I got into electronic music, Nightcore already existed. So I just accepted what I saw at face value. I don't have a very good read on why that became a thing because I wasn't there before it. For me personally, I've pitched up my voice in a lot of songs because I'm not a strong or confident singer so pitching my vocals allows me to feel some distance from my natural singing voice and it gives me something to hide behind. I've been consciously trying to do it less and less as a confidence exercise. I'm just getting more comfortable in general. I guess originally it occured naturally when you speed up an audio file the pitch goes up as well because you're raising the frequency of the waveform which also raises the pitch so if you like physically do that on like a turn table it naturally pitches up. That was an artifact of that technology that people liked and then implemented even when the technology advanced beyond.

MIKE SUNDAY: Yeah, sometimes you get those kinds of crunchy weird artifacts as well, which I think can sometimes be a happy accident when you're sampling. It's funny you bring that up because I know specifically Porter had talked about in some of his earlier albums how he felt like he had to pitch up his vocals or add a glitch effect almost as a mode of self-defense. When I think about a song like “Sing Good”, it feels really raw and honest. I've tried writing my own songs before in a past life, but it's almost embarrassing in a way to try and conceptualize those raw lyrics. In your most recent work, I've seen the lyricism come such a far way. How did you start to make that leap into these really emotional lyrics? Do you have any tips for someone who might be trying to write a more raw honest song?
Nina: Yeah, I mean for me I've written songs and lyrics since I was really young, like primary school age, but I just didn't show them to people and especially when I first got into music production I was trying to make instrumental music. I didn't even think to pair my voice with it. Singing was so far out of the realm of possibility in my mind of things that I was capable of. All of my first productions were kind of bootleg edits and stuff. First, I realized I could put my voice on songs when I started working with my friend Kota Banks because she was the first vocalist who I worked with. So before I started working with Kota, I'd only really made music by myself ever and then I started making music with her and that was my first experience of making music collaboratively with a vocalist in the room that's not just like an acapella. So I was learning so much from working with her and she's also very skilled and very convicted about how she wants her voice to sound and what kind of takes she likes. I learned so much from her being like, can you actually just make this sound like this and I'll be like okay “Yes boss I will!”. I was just learning so much from working with and over that time we also became best friends. This was like, my god like seven years ago now but yeah I learned and then from learning how to produce her voice the way that she wanted me to. Because even though Kota is also an amazing vocal producer and arranger. So I learned so much about that side of things from her then from learning that I was like, if I can treat her vocals this way, I could also just apply that to my own voice and then add a little bit more because I'm not as good of a singer. Her voice does not need all that. She sounds amazing. I learnt the tools from working with her that I then realised I could apply to my own voice. If there are people who write really vulnerable songs but feeling unconfident about putting them out there, the best thing for me was just learning how to make myself sound the way I wanted. You might have to do takes and comp it all together to get the take you like. But if you know how to pitch correct and do the effects, doubles and harmonies and all of those kinds of things, anyone who just records like a single one take vocal with no effects is going to sound less strong than if they put the effects and put the doubles and put the harmonies and zhuzh it all up. So that’s the best thing for it. Anyone who's writing songs who wants to put them out, but feels nervous, learning about vocal production will be a good skill to have.

   

MIKE SUNDAY: I love that. I think there's a certain confidence, even if it may not be how you want to sound, if someone else hears it and they're like, oh, there's a legitimacy to this since it sounds so polished. I know that obviously you work with a lot of other producers, whether it's underscores, 2Charm, or MGNA Crrrta. Are there any production quirks that you have, that someone else has noticed and they're like, “Why do you do it that way? That's so weird”? I'm a graphic designer and sometimes I see someone else do design. I think “I would never do that way.” Has anyone ever called you out for any weird production quirks?
Nina: That's a good question. Maybe! It's interesting seeing how different producers do vocal chops or vocal rearrangements because there's a few different ways to do it. I mean, it's like the tale as old as time, like audio versus MIDI war. But it's funny seeing different producers do vocal chops with MIDI. A lot of the time I'll see someone's session and they've done it with audio and then we'll talk about that and be like this is why I do it this way. I don't feel like anyone's called me out necessarily, but I've noticed most people I've worked with do audio chops. I am a big big MIDI fan. Well, it's like MIDI that's triggering audio. I'm not talking about a VST MIDI, more like the MIDI as a data trigger for audio samples and stuff. I love to do it that way.

MIKE SUNDAY: I feel like it's such a tribe. Some people love to see the waveforms and exactly how it's sort of being chopped up and other people are just “let me put it into a MIDI instrument.”

MIKE SUNDAY: Are there any no-nos when it comes to going back to back? Because I know a lot of the times you're probably DJing with all these other people. Are there any pet peeves? Like, I wish you didn't do that. Or, why did you cut that song off so early?
Nina: I think it's like with anything, good communication can solve any problem. So if I'm going back to back with someone and the song they're playing has this really epic second drop that I don't know about and I'll go to mix in my song and they're like “wait just like just wait, and then I'm like okay i got you!” Usually if we just kind of communicate then then that solves all the problems. All the people I've gone back to back with, at least in recent memory, have been my friends that have really similar tastes and sensibilities. We kind of know when something is good or bad. The biggest no-no would be like, don't pick a bad song, but that's totally subjective. And if you have the right B2B partner, that would never happen.

MIKE SUNDAY: Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. Speaking of [one of your] B2B partners, umru, he's a fantastic graphic designer. I think graphic design, it's such a massive part of your aesthetic, whether it's your avatars, your album covers. Can you talk a little bit about how you work with graphic design, even though your primary medium is audio? How do you think about visual design?
Nina: Yeah, I mean the designer I work with most closely is John You and he designed this *pulls out necklace of ninajirachi avatar I got this from a fan in Miami, this logo and this little guy that's on everything. The little widget guy, so that's John's design. It's collaborative so we go back and forth on stuff but he's the main guy behind my merch and flyers and vinyl, the inside of vinyl inserts and those kinds of assets. The show visuals are made by a bunch of different people, but a lot of the time they're interpreting his assets as well.

MIKE SUNDAY: So does John have a vision and then he sort of goes away and then he shows it to you or is it more of like a step-by-step sort of collaboration?
Nina: It's pretty step-by-step collaborative. At this point we've worked together for a couple of years so he knows what I like and I know how he works but when there's something coming up I might send him an idea of what I want and then he'll make an interpretation that incorporates things that he likes as well and then he'll send it back to me and then a lot of the time I'll just put it in Photoshop and do like a really janky, like janky as fuck, edit to be like, what if we actually move this here or we change this color and then I'll send him back this janky screenshot and he'll just then reinterpret that again. We go back and forth a bit but his greatest skill is interpreting and translating and finding the middle ground between what I want and what he knows is good. He's amazing.

   

MIKE SUNDAY: It's so nice when you're able to find that sort of collaborative partner that you can just really trust and help build out the world. It makes such a difference.
Nina: Totally. I should definitely mention Aria [Zarzycki] too who shot my album cover. She did the Info Hazard video and she also organizes a lot of my show visuals and stuff. It's a similar process with her but on different assets. More video based and photo and video based kind of assets. Those are the two main visual collaborators.

MIKE SUNDAY: That makes a lot of sense. Especially thinking of your album cover. Hardware is such a big part of [your aesthetic], and there's all these people nostalgia baiting and bringing Nintendo DSs to shows and stuff, and people are calling it performative. Does performative even exist, or what do you think about all that stuff? Has anyone brought a DS to your show?
Nina: My god, every single show. I signed a DS last night. Yeah, a lot of DSs. I think everything is a performance really, but not even in any kind of shady way. Even right now in this interview, I'm performing to you, a version of myself that is based on this kind of conversation. Everything is a performance, it just depends who you're performing for and what the intention is. So sometimes when people say that's performative as if it's a negative thing. I think what they actually mean is like that person is giving a performance for a reason that they think is bad. It's not that, because I think everything is performative really, but it doesn't mean it's good or bad. There can be good or bad intentions behind certain performances. If someone wants to film my show on a Nintendo DS because that makes them happy, that's cool. And they're not doing anything wrong. Some people think being performative is bad because they see someone performing a version of themselves that's maybe like inauthentic or they're giving a performance in order to obtain something or do you know what I mean?

MIKE SUNDAY: I think what's interesting too is people will go, “They're a LARPER!” But what's interesting to me is the performative thing has actually exposed things to a lot of people. Just because someone wasn't around for the peak era of DS or CDs or vinyl doesn't mean that they can't appreciate it anymore. So I think that even in being performative, you can gain a legitimate appreciation for whatever that is. It's just one of those internet things that people like to toss around. Speaking of DS, I know you've mentioned Ad Nauseam, Pokemon Mystery Dungeon. There's this inexplicable kind of energy, I even think MapleStory has it: these moods or these save point types of things. Would you ever be into scoring a game? Have you ever thought about that?
Nina: Yes! Absolutely, my whole life I have thought about that. It would be so awesome. I would be really interested to learn about the parameters of video game music scoring because there are limitations, especially with DS music. When I was younger and I learned about soundfonts, I started downloading a bunch and using them. I would be really interested to learn about the limitations of music production for games. I imagine as technology has progressed now, you can just have full whatever in the game because there's more storage on a card. But that 8-bit music came out of a technological limitation. Now it's like a whole thing so that's really interesting to me. I would love to learn more about it and be a part of that for a game someday!

MIKE SUNDAY: Yeah! Put it out into the universe! In music, graphics, I think a lot of the games that we like aren't necessarily what you would call the most technologically impressive thing, but there is something to be said about having those sorts of limitations and that's kind of where creativity is able to butt up where technology ends. Do you self-impose any limitations when you're in the studio, just as a creativity exercise?
Nina: Yes, I do actually and so many ideas and important... I'm trying to think of how to word this. For example, the whole idea of the rave stab would not exist without a technological limitation because that came from taking one slice of audio that's a chord: that has tonal information, it's not just one note. It's a minor chord or whatever and playing that back. So it gets that eerie out key feel to it because you couldn't play it across the 12 notes. Once the technology moved beyond the need, there was no longer that limitation. People were like, “But actually I like how that sounds.” And that would have never existed without the limitations. It's the same way now people want to film on a DS. They don't have to. They could bring a thousand dollar camera and take videos on that. Or an iPhone can film like 4K, but people lack the limitation.

MIKE SUNDAY: Yeah, there's beauty in it.
Nina: Yeah, 100 % like all people love VHS and digital artifacts. When I made my album, I did consciously try to, for the sake of cohesion. For instance, I had this song finished and then I was finishing this song over here, and this song was missing a bass. I'd be like okay, instead of trying to reinvent the wheel I'm actually just gonna take the bass from this song and adapt it for this song so it feels like the same band played the whole album if that makes sense. That was the only real main limitation I placed though.

MIKE SUNDAY: So are you someone that likes to try out new VSTs and new tools, or once you’ve figured out your tools, “Okay, these are my bass patches, and these are my stabs” do you just stick to those tools?
Nina: I like to rinse something to death before moving on from it and really get to a point, where I'm really struggling for any good ideas out of this thing I've used so much. And then I'll be like, okay, maybe it's time to download something else and for the sake of getting new inspiration and stuff. I like to really see a piece of software out before I download something new.

MIKE SUNDAY: Really push it to its limits. You know the instrument inside and out. You had mentioned the scene growing up in Australia. I think maybe less so now, but did you ever feel like EDM and the music you were into was more North American focused? There’s this kind of this “third spaces" idea for a lot of these internet kids. Their first time being connected with other people is through the internet. So where were you hanging out? Was it YouTube? You talked about SoundCloud and forums. What were those early internet third spaces for you?
Nina: YouTube and SoundCloud were the biggest ones for sure. For EDM, it was kind of a whole world thing. Even a lot of my favourite music when I was younger was Australian. For example, WaveRacer, who I now work with on mixing. I heard his music for the first time when I was about 13 or 14 and I was like, my God. He became one of my favourite artists very quickly and he was from Australia. But even still, the world of Australian music felt very far out of my reach especially because I wasn't from a big city or anything. A lot of the music I got into when I was younger was also European or British. PC music is a British label or Cashmere Cat is European, even Fractal Fantasy is like Canadian European. Flume for example? I can't believe I didn't think of Flume. Flume is Australian as well. Hudson Mohawk. [My favorite music] is from all over the world. SoundCloud and YouTube were my biggest entry points for sure. Those old algorithms would show me a lot of cool stuff.

MIKE SUNDAY: Let's go! Shout out Flume! Was there anything that you saw as a kid that you were definitely too young to see that you still have seared in your memory?
Nina: Yes, I have a little song about it! I don't know if it's very classy to describe what I saw but a lot of stuff that scarred me about the internet. A lot of it I actually didn't see first-person. It would be the boys on the bus talking about or watching it right next to me. I'd be like, “I'm not looking at that.”

MIKE SUNDAY: That's relatable! Someone always had an older brother that showed them a weird liveleak video that you definitely shouldn't have been seeing at that age. Technology right now is, it feels quite dystopic, especially with things like AI and just the way the world is going. It feels very much like The Wired in Serial Experiments Lain. But in your lyrics, you talk about these things like online and digital identity and sentient computers and even AI to a certain degree. Why was depicting this warmth and this intimacy so important to you? Versus this cold technology that everyone wants to believe?
Nina: Yeah, it's so funny. I never want people to think that I'm just looking back at the internet of the past and being like “oh life was so much better when I was 13” because it was not. It's definitely better now. For me I don't need to go back to being 13, but the reason I look back at it so fondly isn't because I want to go back in time. My high school friends are still my best friends, but all of my friends that I've made post high school, I've been connected to through music and the internet. I think about how, if my world was limited to the hometown I grew up in without the internet, I would have never discovered computer music or made the friends that I have through the shared love of computer music. I got to do that because I had internet access. Maybe the trade-off was seeing some fucked up video that I'll never forget, but for me that was a price I was happy to pay because I love electronic music so much. Even just earlier in our chat we were talking about the concept of like, me, I'm from Australia and Ramon is Filipino-American living in LA and we were doing a tour together in Japan with Heaven's Gate and we all grew up listening to the same music on SoundCloud and we all met through the internet and then we're there in person having an amazing Japanese dinner with the promoters and we're talking about Fractal Fantasy. And it's just like, wow, this is so cool that I get to have this experience and I would not get to have it if I didn't have a computer when I was younger and have access to the world outside of my hometown. That's why I look back at it so fondly because it's like, wow, those discoveries that I made on the internet when I was little really signposted my life. At the time it just felt electric. I was like “What is this music?” I had no idea what I was gonna do after school. I just went with what I liked. I know it's very like myopic. I wasn't trying to make an album that was a grand statement about the general state of technology. I have this gratitude. It was just about my experience.

item.title: Japan Built Different: sabukaru’s Love Letter to Contemporary Japanese Architecture
item.dc:creator: Abeer S
item.description:
Japan’s architectural archive spans millennia; the approach developed by Japanese architects has resonated globally from the late 20th century into the present day. While no single description can capture the multitude of styles found within modern Japanese architecture, aspects of Japanese culture and worldview remain a common thread throughout these works. For many Japanese architects, integration with nature, both through the surrounding environment and the use of natural materials, remains a central theme. 

   

Contemporary Japanese architecture is guided by enduring principles that remain deeply connected to its traditional roots, with tradition and modernity existing as parts of the same spectrum. Contemporary architects closely study architectural legacy, refine it into essential principles, and translate it into contemporary contexts. From the principle of Ma, or meaningful emptiness, to Wabi-Sabi, the appreciation of imperfection, and Shakkei, the practice of borrowing surrounding scenery to create serene and functional environments, these philosophies allow architects to blend historical sensitivity with modern innovation.

   

With nine Pritzker Prize winners, often considered architecture’s equivalent of the Nobel Prize, Japan stands as a global force in architectural thought, influencing generations through its fusion of traditional wisdom and futuristic vision. Within this article, sabukaru highlights the architects who shaped the legacy of contemporary Japanese architecture beyond the realm of buildings alone, creating spaces that continue to influence how people perceive both the world and themselves.

Tadao Ando 

 









The story of one of the world's most renowned architects is a pretty interesting one.

Tadao Ando was headed for a boxing career when architecture found him, not through a school or a mentor but through a used bookstore and a teenage encounter with Frank Lloyd Wright's Imperial Hotel in Tokyo that rearranged his sense of what was possible. He had shown real promise in the ring, fought professionally, and might have continued down that path had he not watched former world champion Fighting Harada spar one day and walked away knowing the limits of where natural talent alone could take someone. "I was overwhelmed," he said. Boxing left him with what observers would later describe as a stoic perseverance and a quiet fighting spirit, but the sport had made its point, and architecture was already pulling harder.

The education that followed had no institution behind it. Ando found a monograph on Le Corbusier in a used bookstore and began tracing the drawings of his early period so many times that all the pages turned black. He took correspondence courses in interior design, read constantly, and from the age of eighteen began visiting the temples, shrines, and tea houses of Kyoto and Nara to study spatial experience directly. "I was studying architecture by going to see actual buildings, and reading books about them," he said, a method that would eventually take him across Europe and America to stand in front of the structures he had only known through pages. Le Corbusier's geometry in Marseille landed particularly hard; the encounter with built modernism confirmed something he had been working toward in solitude for years.

A vivid ray of light entering his home during renovations became another turning point, a moment that crystallized what he wanted architecture to do, not just shelter people but move them, creating spaces where light and shadow do the emotional work that words cannot. That philosophy became the foundation of everything that followed. Ando's approach centers on the precise manipulation of concrete, light, and spatial voids, building enclosed environments that separate the individual from the noise of the city while connecting them to natural phenomena, light shifting through the day, wind moving through a corridor, rain audible against a surface, and sky visible through a calculated opening. The synthesis he arrived at brought together Western modernism, specifically Le Corbusier's geometry, with Japanese spatial concepts rooted in ma and wabi-sabi, producing architecture that is simultaneously rational and transcendent, ordered and deeply felt.

The work earned him the Pritzker Prize in 1994, architecture's highest honor, and confirmed what the buildings had already been saying for years. At 85 in 2026, Ando's firm continues to design significant work around the world, the output of someone who never stopped moving toward the thing that stopped him cold in a used bookstore decades ago: a set of traced drawings and the conviction that space could change how a person experiences being alive.

Toyo Ito



















Just like the preceding, architecture was not in the plan for Toyo Ito. Baseball was his passion, engineering his intention, and architecture his fallback when his grades at the University of Tokyo left him with limited options. What happened next contradicted all of that completely, his undergraduate proposal for the redesign of Ueno Park taking the top prize at the university and signaling that the reluctant architecture student had found something worth pursuing after all.

Born in Seoul in 1941 and raised in Japan after his family returned when he was two, Ito grew up around people who had a quiet relationship with making and building, a grandfather who dealt in lumber, and a father who liked drawing plans for friends' houses. None of it translated into a conscious ambition toward architecture, but the exposure left something behind.

Where Tadao Ando reached for heavy concrete and shadow, Ito moved in the opposite direction, toward lightness, air, and at times near-translucence. The Tower of Winds outside Yokohama Station captures this perfectly, a tubular structure that reads as industrial during the day and transforms completely at night through LED lamps, neon rings, and floodlights whose illumination is controlled entirely by wind speed and ambient noise. Nature determines what the building shows, making the architecture alive in a way that no fixed design could achieve.

That relationship between structure and natural environment deepened across his career. The Sendai Mediatheque, completed in 2001 and one of Ito's own most cherished projects, was built around thirteen tubes penetrating flat concrete slabs with walls kept to an absolute minimum, producing a public building that dissolved the fixed barriers between programs and let the space breathe and redistribute itself freely. For Ito, the grid that defined twentieth-century architecture had made cities and the people within them homogenous, and his work across four decades was a sustained attempt to find a different relationship between buildings and their surroundings.

The 2011 earthquake and tsunami brought that philosophy into its most human dimension. Ito joined a group of architects in developing Home-for-All, communal spaces built for survivors living in conditions that offered neither privacy nor comfort. The project returned him to the most fundamental question architecture could ask: why a building is made and for whom, a question he argued modern architecture had forgotten in its pursuit of originality. 

His museum on the island of Omishima in the Seto Inland Sea, opened in 2011 and designed by Ito himself, now holds his past projects and serves as a workshop for young architects, a fitting continuation from someone who never planned to be an architect and spent a career redefining what the discipline could mean.

SANAA (Kazuyo Sejima + Ryue Nishizawa)


















Founded by Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa, SANAA operates from a deceptively simple premise: that a building is not finished when the architects leave, but when the people arrive. The studio has spent three decades designing spaces that dissolve the boundary between inside and outside, structure and light, architecture and the life unfolding within it, and the results have reshaped what public and cultural spaces are allowed to be.

Both Sejima and Nishizawa came up through Toyo Ito's office, where they first crossed paths before forming their own partnership. That lineage matters, the influence of Ito's lightness and structural experimentation running visibly through SANAA's work, pushed further toward transparency and social openness. Their buildings are stripped of anything that competes with the people inside them, white, glass, softly curved, deliberately empty of elaboration so that the space becomes a canvas for whoever inhabits it. The absence of material excess is not a limitation but the entire point, architecture functioning as a blank surface that activates rather than dictates.

What sets SANAA apart is how rigorously that philosophy holds across wildly different scales and contexts. The New Museum in New York stacks its volumes with a casual confidence that somehow still feels considered. The Rolex Learning Center in Lausanne curves and undulates across a single floor, creating a landscape rather than a floor plan. The Louvre-Lens sits in the French countryside with a stillness that makes the art inside feel inevitable. Each project starts from the same question: how does a building encourage people to meet, move, and be present, and each one finds a different answer without abandoning the framework that makes SANAA's work immediately recognizable.

Kenzo Tange














Kenzo Tange sits at the foundation of contemporary Japanese architecture, the figure from whom so much of what followed can be traced. His entry into the discipline came through a magazine, a photograph of Le Corbusier's work spotted in 1935 that shifted the direction of everything that came after. He absorbed modernism through the office of Kunio Maekawa, a former Le Corbusier disciple, before developing something that could only have come from Japan, a synthesis of Western structural logic and a deeply rooted spatial tradition that he spent a career refining into what he called lyrical brutalism, concrete used not as a blunt material but as something capable of appealing to the human heart.

At the center of Tange's philosophy was a conviction he described as the dialectical synthesis of tradition and anti-tradition, the idea that genuine creation holds both in tension without resolving into either. Tradition, in his thinking, functions as a catalyst, present in the making and undetectable in the result, a force that shapes without being seen. That principle runs through everything he built, buildings that feel unmistakably Japanese and entirely of their moment at the same time, rooted without being historical, modern without being rootless.

The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and Park became his first major commission and his international introduction, the building's radical simplicity carrying the weight of what it commemorated through restraint rather than gesture. Tange also championed the Metabolism movement, which understood buildings and cities as organic, evolving structures capable of changing over time, applying biological logic to urban form. His 1960 proposal to expand Tokyo across the bay with enormous modular structures took that thinking to its most ambitious scale, radical, unbuilt, and decades ahead of how cities would eventually start thinking about growth and flexibility.

The Yoyogi National Gymnasium, built for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, became the fullest expression of his architectural philosophy, a suspended roof structure in steel, glass, and concrete that evoked a pagoda and a spacecraft simultaneously, functional and monumental, modern and deeply rooted. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building followed, its twin tower design earning the nickname Notre Dame de Tokyo, demonstrating how far Tange's vocabulary could stretch without losing its essential character.

Beyond the buildings, Tange shaped the discipline through the Tange Laboratory at Tokyo University, and treated image-making as an extension of architectural thinking, photographing his own projects and those of his inspirations extensively.

Sou Fujimoto












Sou Fujimoto grew up in the forests of Hokkaido, and his origin never left his thinking. The experience of moving through trees, of space that has no clear boundary between inside and outside, open and enclosed, became the foundation of everything he would later build and write, a philosophy he calls Primitive Future, the conviction that the most advanced architecture might be the kind that returns to something elemental.

Before architecture, Fujimoto had wanted to be a physicist. Einstein was his inspiration, the questions about space, light, and the nature of perception pulling him toward the University of Tokyo until he redirected into architecture and found in Le Corbusier the same quality of thinking he had admired in scientists. The subject changed, but the questions stayed the same, and that scientific curiosity about the fundamental nature of space runs through everything he has built since.

At the center of his philosophy is the idea of a third space, neither pure nature nor pure architecture but an integration of both, environments that replicate the non-linear, interconnected experience of moving through a forest rather than navigating a series of defined rooms. Fujimoto describes his architecture as simultaneously a forest and a cave, two spatial experiences that seem opposite but share the same quality of being immersive, ambient, and impossible to fully read from a single vantage point. That ambiguity is deliberate. He builds spaces that resist immediate comprehension, where the boundary between interior and exterior, between floor and wall, and between furniture and public and private, dissolves into something more continuous and open-ended.

His concept of Primitive Future holds that architecture's most progressive move is not forward into abstraction but backward into instinct, toward the spatial logic that existed before rooms had names and functions were fixed. The repetition that runs through his structures, vertical lines, modular grids, stacked elements, is never purely formal but always in service of that rhythm, the way a forest repeats its own pattern without ever producing the same space twice. Transparency and weightlessness are not aesthetic preferences but philosophical positions; a building that seems to disappear into its surroundings is a building that has stopped insisting on itself, and for Fujimoto, that restraint is where architecture becomes most alive.

Abeer Salah is a Seoul-based editor, writer, and cultural curator exploring emerging scenes, underground culture, and internet-born subcultures. She is the founder of the collective P.T.S.D.
